meta.title_plain: How a kid who loved coding built Fortnite
meta.teaser: Tim Sweeney coded for 10,000 hours before his first big game.

page.title: How a kid who loved coding built Fortnite
page.sub: Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney on the Lex Fridman Podcast
page.bigIdea: Tim Sweeney coded for about 10,000 hours before his first big game. Huge things start as lots of small projects.

cards.title: It started at age 11
cards.front: Tim's older brother showed him a computer, and he was hooked.
cards.back: He learned to code in a few days. From age 10 to 20, he spent about 10,000 hours building his own projects.
cards.tryit: Pick one small thing to build this week: a game, a map or a website.

cards.title: Games are puzzles to solve
cards.front: Tim played games to figure out how they worked.
cards.back: When Doom came out, he moved the mouse pixel by pixel to see how it was drawn. Then he built his own version.
cards.tryit: Next time you play, ask: how did they make that work?

cards.title: His first company ran from home
cards.front: At about 20, he sold his game ZZT from his parents' house.
cards.back: Players mailed in orders, and he made around $100 a day. His secret: he gave players the editor so they could build their own levels.
cards.tryit: Think of something you could make that other people can build on.

cards.title: 6 months turned into 3.5 years
cards.front: Epic planned to make its first 3D game in six months.
cards.back: It took three and a half years, and they almost ran out of money. They kept going, and Unreal Engine now powers huge games and even movies.
cards.tryit: When a project takes longer than planned, keep improving it instead of quitting.

cards.title: Fortnite began as a 1-week experiment
cards.front: Fortnite started in 2011 as a one-week game jam.
cards.back: The idea: build forts by day, fight zombies by night. Years later, the team made Battle Royale in about four weeks, and it exploded.
cards.tryit: Hold your own game jam: give yourself one week to make something fun.

words.d: Someone who writes code to tell computers what to do.
The toolkit used to build games, like Unreal Engine.
Give part of a game away free, then sell the rest.
A short challenge to build a game fast, often in days.

quiz.q: About how many hours did Tim code before his first big game?
quiz.hint: Look at the big idea at the top.
quiz.why: Around 10,000 hours, from age 10 to 20. Skill comes from lots of practice.
It began in 2011 as a week-long experiment about forts and zombies.

quiz.q: What did Tim give ZZT players that made it so popular?
opts: The editor to build their own levels
quiz.hint: Fortnite Creative does the same thing today.
quiz.why: Letting players create their own levels kept the community growing.

quiz.q: Unreal was planned for 6 months. How long did it really take?
quiz.why: 3.5 years. Big projects almost always take longer, so keep going.

page.think: Tim says it's smarter to make something new than to copy what's already popular. What's a game or project idea that nobody has made yet?
